prose.def: The practice of sorcery or witchcraft, often involving magic potions or spells.
prose.article: In the New Testament, φαρμακεία always appears with the meaning "sorcery" or "witchcraft" — all 3 Byzantine occurrences (Galatians 5:20, Revelation 9:21, 18:23) are rendered that way. A vivid example comes from the papyri: an Egyptian document from B.C. 258 has a man explaining he can't leave the house because a dose of medicine has made him sick, while a later record (A.D. 131) uses the same word to accuse a mother of poisoning.

prose.def: Describes something subject to decay and corruption—perishable or corruptible—in contrast to what is imperishable and eternal.
prose.article: φθαρτός describes anything liable to decay and destruction—a withering athlete's wreath, money that wears out, the human body that dies. The New Testament uses it 6 times, and translators render it "perishable" in 5 cases and "mortal" once (Rom 1:23), but these are really the same idea seen from two angles. Notably, it is built directly from φθείρω ("to destroy, corrupt") and is repeatedly set in deliberate contrast with its opposite ἄφθαρτος, the imperishable, as when it labels mortal humanity against the immortal God.

Abbott-Smith's note that the plural is the normal form (except Isaiah 19:17) demonstrates the definition should foreground the plural, since the NT evidence is exclusively plural
